tagline.text: A hot spring village at the foot of Mount Makiling in Laguna

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱110~25,000 (from day-use entry for one person at a public spring to one night in a private villa for a group)

children.text: Pansol is a hot spring village in Calamba beneath Mount Makiling, packed with hot spring resorts and private villas. It is about
1–1.5 hours
from Manila by car, so it suits both a day soak and an overnight group getaway.
Pansol is a barangay at the southeastern edge of Calamba City in Laguna, at the foot of Mount Makiling. According to Wikipedia it covers
about 5.28 km²

and had 12,099 residents in the 2024 census. The name is said to come from the Tagalog word pansol, meaning "spring," and the village lives up to it. Calamba is nicknamed the "Spring Resort Capital of the Philippines," and its resorts cluster in barangays such as Pansol, Bucal and Bagong Kalsada, with Pansol the best known of them.

Pansol is not a single park with one entrance ticket; the whole village is a hot spring district. Resort signs line the lanes, and they fall into two broad types. One is the public resort where you pay an entrance fee and spend the day, and the other is the private resort where you rent a whole villa with its own hot spring pool. Wikipedia says the village has drawn resort visitors since the 1970s and had about 700 resorts as of October 2009. The number is clearly still very large, but the exact count depends on when you ask.

The water is groundwater heated by the geothermal activity of Mount Makiling. The mountain is a dormant volcano with no recorded historic eruption, yet hot springs and mud springs show that heat remains underground. Water color and temperature differ slightly from resort to resort. At the public Laguna Hot Spring Resort, the water looks brown because of the sandy bottom, but it is described as regularly tested and safe to soak in. The idea that the mineral-rich water eases muscle aches and helps the skin is a local belief rather than a proven effect, so think of it as a place to relax.
Being close to Manila is Pansol's biggest advantage. Calamba, about
50km
south of Manila, is connected by SLEX and usually takes
1–1.5 hours

when traffic is light. That is why families and friends, including Korean residents of the Philippines, often come for a weekend day trip or a one-night gathering. Because it is so popular, though, weekends and holidays are crowded and the village roads clog up, so allow plenty of travel time when planning.

blocks.title: A day soak at a public hot spring resort

children.text: You pay an entrance fee and move between several hot spring pools, which is the most affordable way to enjoy Pansol. Laguna Hot Spring Resort is a typical example, and places such as Sun City and Southwinds are also described as budget-friendly public pools. Cabins and tables are often rented separately from the entrance fee.

blocks.title: A night in a private villa with your group

children.text: You rent an entire villa with its own pool, rooms, kitchen and karaoke machine. Villas that sleep
20–30 people
are common and popular for family reunions, clubs and company workshops. Rates are often set per villa rather than per person.

This is a long-established mid-sized hot spring complex in the Pansol area. According to its promotional material, it covers about 7 hectares with 9 to 11 hot spring pools, and the hottest pool reaches
. A Korean restaurant and a massage center make it a comfortable choice for Korean travelers.
The best way to soak is to warm up in a hot pool for about
10–15 minutes
at a time and then rest in a cold pool or in the shade. Staying in hot water for more than an hour can cause dizziness, so drink water often.

blocks.title: A whole village at the foot of Mount Makiling

children.text: Pansol lies below Mount Makiling, so many resorts have green mountain slopes in view on a clear day. Walking through the gardens between pools or resting in a cabin while looking at the mountain is part of the pleasure here.

blocks.title: Combining it with Calamba city sights

children.text: From Pansol you can head into Calamba city to see the Rizal Shrine and the roughly
statue of Rizal in the plaza in front of City Hall. Adding one history stop to a day at the springs makes the itinerary richer.

blocks.title: Rest with Korean food and a massage

children.text: Some places, like 88 Hotspring, have a Korean restaurant and massage service, which is good for elderly relatives or families with children who worry about food. Massages usually need a booking, so reserve a slot as soon as you arrive.

items.title: Half-day trip
items.subtitle: A day at a public hot spring

children.text: Take SLEX from Makati or Ortigas and exit at Calamba. On weekends, the earlier you leave, the lighter the traffic.
Arrive at a public hot spring resort, register at the entrance and check the lockers and showers. Reviews of Laguna Hot Spring Resort advise arriving before
on weekends to avoid the crowds.
Grab a shaded cabin or table first and ease in with the lukewarm pools. Then take turns in the hot pool,
10–15 minutes
at a time.
Eat lunch at the resort restaurant or bring a packed meal. Rules on outside food differ by resort, so ask at the entrance.
If you have children, let them play in the shallow pools while adults take a massage or rest.
Shower, pack up and head back to Manila. Northbound SLEX is often congested on Sunday afternoons, so it is better to leave early.
Public springs have low entrance fees but the facilities can be dated and many are crowded, so choose based on recent reviews.
Arrive at the villa and check in. Check-in is usually around
and check-out around noon at many places, but confirm the schedule of the one you booked.
Unpack the groceries and check the rules for the kitchen and grill. Ask in advance which food and drinks may be brought in and whether catering carries extra fees.
Take a first soak in your private hot spring pool before sunset.
Dinner and the party. Most villas have a karaoke machine, but the village has quiet hours, so confirm the rules around
at night.
The next morning, get back into the pool during the cool hours. Have breakfast and pack up.
Check out. Some places charge extra per hour for late check-out, so keep to the time.
Villa rates vary greatly with the number of guests and the day of the week, so get the guest-count basis and inclusions in writing before booking.

items.title: Hot springs and Rizal
items.subtitle: History and relaxation in one day

children.text: Start with the Rizal Shrine, the birthplace of José Rizal, in Calamba city. The museum is open
and closed on Mondays and holidays.
See the Rizal statue in the plaza in front of City Hall and pass by St. John the Baptist Parish Church.
Have lunch in Calamba city, then go to Pansol by jeepney or tricycle.
Enter a public hot spring and enjoy the whole afternoon soaking.
Shower and return to Manila.
Opening hours at the shrine may change, so check the latest notice before you visit.
From Makati or Pasay, take SLEX and exit at Calamba; it takes about
1–1.5 hours
(longer on weekends and Friday evenings).
From Calamba, follow the Maharlika and National Highways toward Mount Makiling. The easiest way is to search for your resort's name in a map app.
Wikivoyage says traffic in Pansol is often congested and that the resorts are more convenient to reach by car. Check in advance whether your resort has parking.
Some places, such as 88 Hotspring, have free parking, but it varies by resort.
Take a bus bound for Calamba, Santa Cruz or Lucena from the Buendia terminals (JAC Liner, JAM, DLTBCo) or PITX Gate 5, and ask to be dropped at Calamba Crossing or near Pansol.
The route planner Rome2Rio estimates about
1 hour 43 minutes
and a fare of ₱230–290 by bus, but confirm the actual fare and time at the terminal.
After getting off, continue to the resort by jeepney or tricycle.
Bus routes and terminals change often, so check before you leave.
The Philippine National Railways (PNR) Metro Commuter Line has Calamba station and Pansol station (a flag stop).
Rome2Rio lists a train from Paco to Calamba once a day taking about
3.5 hours
, but service status changes a lot, so check the latest PNR notice if you plan to take the train.
You can reach anywhere in Pansol by tricycle, with stands near the subdivision entrances. Wikivoyage gives the fare as about ₱9 per kilometer and about ₱60 for a special (solo) trip.
From Calamba city, a jeepney toward Pansol, Makiling and UP Los Baños costs about ₱20 and takes
20 minutes to 1 hour
. Board at SM Calamba or the Calamba central terminal.
You can soak all year round, but because you spend long hours resting at outdoor pools, the dry season with less rain is more comfortable. By the Philippines' general climate pattern,
November–May
is the dry season, and
November–February
is relatively cool, which is nice for hot water.

What matters more than the weather is the crowds. Public springs are packed on weekends, holidays, Holy Week and the year-end season, and villa bookings fill early, so groups should book several weeks ahead. Weekdays are usually less crowded than weekends, so choose a weekday if your schedule is flexible.

There are two ways to stay. Some public hot springs have rooms, but renting a large pool villa is the typical way to stay overnight in Pansol. Many pool villas have kitchens, so you can bring groceries and cook, and you should check in advance whether you can call a caterer.

For meals, eat at the resort restaurant or shop for groceries in Calamba city or near SM Calamba. Some places, like 88 Hotspring Resort, run a Korean restaurant and a Filipino grill restaurant together. When booking a villa, always get the rules on outside food and drinks, grill use, quiet hours and deposits by text or messenger.
There are so many resorts that choosing is hard at first. Decide on the date, group size and budget, compare recent reviews of two or three places, and then get in touch.
Many small springs accept cash only, so bring plenty of small bills.
Group bookings usually ask for a deposit up front, with the balance due on arrival. The deposit can be non-refundable, so check the terms.
For villas, check the guest-count basis in the price list, the extra-guest fee, and whether the overnight capacity differs from the day-use capacity.
Bring towels, toiletries, a change of clothes and slippers, and leave valuables in a locker. Some resorts charge a locker deposit.
Enter hot pools for short stints and drink water often. Do not get into a hot pool after drinking alcohol.
Karaoke machines can usually be used, but Pansol guides say many resorts impose quiet hours between
and
. Check the exact time with the place you booked.
Roads in the village clog easily, so leave early to arrive in time for check-in.
Rates and rules differ from place to place in Pansol and change often, and some listings are out of date, so always confirm the latest rates and rules with the resort before booking.
Much of the information is dated. Entrance was listed at ₱50–100 around 2023 and at ₱110–150 in 2026, so treat prices in reviews only as a guide.
Water condition and upkeep vary by resort. Some places look dated, so check recent reviews and photos.
Pregnant women, people with heart or blood pressure conditions and young children should avoid staying long in hot pools. If you are worried about your health, consult a doctor beforehand.

Wikivoyage notes that some of the southernmost barangays of Calamba fall within the danger radius of a major Taal Volcano eruption. It is not confirmed whether Pansol is included, so check volcano status announcements.
Leave valuables in a locker and do not leave them at the pool edge or in a cabin.
This is the mountain at whose foot Pansol lies. Pansol is near the Los Baños boundary, so it is easy to continue to the mountain and the Los Baños area after your soak.
This is the house where José Rizal was born. Admission is free with donations accepted, and it is closed on Mondays and holidays. It is a good history stop to add to a day at the springs.
This is a hot spring in tropical rainforest between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. If you want a forest-style hot spring, this place in the same province of Laguna suits you better.
This amusement park in Santa Rosa lies along SLEX on the way back to Manila. One Pansol villa listing puts it about 13 miles (about
21 km
) away.
